chapters.title: Light - Reflection and Refraction
chapters.summary: This chapter covers reflection of light by spherical mirrors and refraction by spherical lenses: image formation with ray diagrams, the Cartesian sign convention, mirror and lens formulae, magnification and power of a lens. Refractive index and Snell's law complete the optics base, and step-wise numericals on image position, size and nature carry most of the 7-mark board weightage.

sections.heading: Reflection of Light and Spherical Mirrors
points: Laws of reflection: the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane, and the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (angle i = angle r).
A spherical mirror is part of a hollow sphere: with the inner surface reflecting it is a concave (converging) mirror, and with the outer surface reflecting it is a convex (diverging) mirror.

Basic terms: pole P is the centre of the mirror surface, centre of curvature C is the centre of the parent sphere, principal focus F is the point where rays parallel to the principal axis actually meet (concave) or appear to meet (convex) after reflection.

Focal length formula (write it on its own): f = R/2 for both types of spherical mirrors; the focal length of a concave mirror is negative and that of a convex mirror is positive in the Cartesian convention.

A plane mirror always forms a virtual, erect, same-size, laterally inverted image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front; a plane mirror can be treated as a spherical mirror of infinite focal length.
Common mistake: the angle of incidence is measured from the NORMAL, not from the mirror surface, so a ray making 40 degrees with the mirror surface has an angle of incidence of 50 degrees.

keyTerms.meaning: The central point of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror; all distances in formulae are measured from it.
The point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis converge (concave mirror) or appear to diverge from (convex mirror) after reflection.
The radius of the sphere of which the mirror is a part; the focal length is half of it, f = R/2.

sections.trick: f is always half of R: f = R/2. And angles live on the normal, never on the mirror surface.
sections.examPointer: CBSE asks 1 to 2 mark items on the laws of reflection, f = R/2 and the choice of mirrors for specific uses; always quote angle i = angle r and specify that angles are measured from the normal.

sections.heading: Image Formation by Spherical Mirrors (Ray Diagrams in Words)
points: Standard rays: a ray parallel to the principal axis passes through F after reflection in a concave mirror (or appears to come from F for a convex mirror); a ray through F returns parallel to the axis; a ray through C retraces its own path; a ray hitting the pole reflects symmetrically about the axis.
Concave mirror with object beyond C: image forms between F and C, real, inverted and diminished; with the object at infinity the image is at F, real, inverted and point-sized.
Concave mirror with object at C: image at C itself, real, inverted and of the same size, so the magnification is -1.
Concave mirror with object between F and C: image beyond C, real, inverted and enlarged; with the object at F the image is at infinity, real, inverted and highly enlarged.
Concave mirror with object between P and F: image behind the mirror, virtual, erect and enlarged; this is the shaving-mirror and dentist-mirror case.

Convex mirror: for every object position the image lies between P and F behind the mirror, virtual, erect and diminished; as the object moves away the image shrinks towards F, which is exactly why rear-view mirrors use convex mirrors.

keyTerms.meaning: Formed by the actual intersection of reflected rays, can be caught on a screen and is always inverted for spherical mirrors.
Formed by the backward extension of reflected rays, cannot be caught on a screen and is erect for spherical mirrors.
Left-right interchange seen in plane mirror images, such as the word AMBULANCE printed in reverse on vehicles.

sections.trick: Concave memory ladder: beyond C small, at C equal, inside C big, inside F virtual-big; convex mirror: always small, always erect, always behind.
sections.examPointer: Ray-diagram questions carry 2 to 3 marks: describe which two standard rays you used, because the examiner checks the rays; finish by naming the image nature in one line for the last mark.

sections.heading: Sign Convention, Mirror Formula and Magnification
points: Cartesian sign convention: the pole is the origin and the principal axis is the x-axis; distances are measured from the pole; distances measured in the direction of incident light are positive and against it are negative; heights above the principal axis are positive and heights below it are negative.
Practical outcomes: the object distance u is always negative; f is negative for a concave mirror and positive for a convex mirror; a real image has negative v and a virtual image has positive v.
Mirror formula (write it on its own): 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, so 1/v = 1/f - 1/u; solve only after rewriting the given data with correct signs.
Mirror magnification (write it on its own): m = h'/h = -v/u; a negative m means the image is real and inverted, a positive m means it is virtual and erect.
Image size: h' = m × h; if the modulus of m is greater than 1 the image is enlarged, if it is less than 1 the image is diminished.
Common mistake: dropping signs is the top error in this chapter; substitute u = -30 and f = -15 exactly as they are, and let the signs of v and m decide the nature of the image instead of guessing.

keyTerms.meaning: The Cartesian rules of signs for distances measured along or against the incident light and for heights above or below the principal axis.
1/v + 1/u = 1/f, connecting object distance, image distance and focal length of a spherical mirror.
Ratio of image height to object height for a mirror, m = h'/h = -v/u.

sections.trick: For mirrors remember RIN - Real Is Negative: real images have negative v and negative m; virtual images come with positive v and positive m.
sections.examPointer: A 3-mark numerical on v, m or f appears in almost every paper: score by writing the given data with signs, the formula, the substitution and the nature of the image as the final line.

sections.heading: Refraction, Snell's Law and Refractive Index
points: Refraction is the change of direction of light when it passes obliquely from one transparent medium to another because its speed changes; entering a denser medium light bends towards the normal, and entering a rarer medium it bends away from the normal.

Laws of refraction: the incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane, and sin i / sin r = constant for a given pair of media and a given colour of light (Snell's law).
Refractive index (write it on its own): n21 = v1/v2, the ratio of the speed of light in medium 1 to that in medium 2; the absolute refractive index is n = c/v with c = 3 × 10^8 m/s.
A larger n means slower light in that medium: glass has n about 1.5 (speed 2 × 10^8 m/s) and water has n about 1.33, that is 4/3 (speed 2.25 × 10^8 m/s).
Relative index relations: n21 × n12 = 1, and the refractive index of glass with respect to water = n(glass)/n(water) = (3/2)/(4/3) = 9/8 = 1.125.
Common mistakes: refractive index has no unit, and it depends on the pair of media and the colour of light, not on the angle of incidence; also an optically denser medium is not necessarily heavier.

keyTerms.meaning: Bending of light when it crosses obliquely into a medium in which its speed is different.
Ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to the speed of light in the medium, n = c/v; a pure number without unit.
The medium with the larger refractive index and hence the smaller speed of light in it.

sections.trick: Dense bends down: into a denser medium the ray bends closer to the normal. And n = c/v: bigger n, slower v. For relative index simply divide the two absolute indices.
sections.examPointer: Expect a 2 to 3 mark question to define refractive index, to find the speed of light in a medium from n, or to state the two laws of refraction with a labelled glass-slab description.

sections.heading: Refraction by Spherical Lenses and Image Formation
points: A convex lens is thicker at the middle, converges rays and has positive focal length; a concave lens is thinner at the middle, diverges rays and has negative focal length; a thin lens has two foci at equal distances on either side of the optical centre O.

Standard rays: a ray parallel to the axis passes through the second focus F2 after refraction (or appears to come from the focus on the incident side for a concave lens); a ray through the optical centre O goes straight; a ray through the first focus F1 emerges parallel to the axis.

Convex lens cases: object at infinity, image at F2, real, inverted, highly diminished; object beyond 2F1, image between F2 and 2F2, real, inverted, diminished; object at 2F1, image at 2F2, real, inverted, same size.

Convex lens cases continued: object between F1 and 2F1, image beyond 2F2, real, inverted, enlarged; object at F1, image at infinity; object between O and F1, image on the same side, virtual, erect, enlarged, which is the magnifying-glass case.
Concave lens: whatever the object position, the image is always between the optical centre and the focus on the same side as the object, virtual, erect and diminished.

Common mistake: 2F of a lens plays the role that C plays for a mirror, and the lens magnification m = v/u has NO minus sign; also for lenses a positive v means a real image on the opposite side, unlike mirrors where positive v means virtual.

keyTerms.meaning: The central point of a thin lens through which a ray passes without any deviation.
Points at distance f on either side of the lens; rays parallel to the axis pass through F2 of a convex lens or appear to come from the focus on the incident side in a concave lens.
Points at twice the focal length; an object at 2F1 forms a same-size real image at 2F2, just as an object at C does for a mirror.

sections.trick: Replace mirror C by lens 2F everywhere. Lens signs: positive v = real (other side), negative v = virtual (same side); m = v/u with no minus sign.
sections.examPointer: Identify-the-nature questions (object position given) and convex versus concave comparisons are common 2 to 3 mark items; answer in one line covering position, real or virtual, erect or inverted, and size.

sections.heading: Lens Formula, Magnification and Power of a Lens
points: Lens formula (write it on its own): 1/v - 1/u = 1/f; rewrite the given data with signs first and then solve for the missing quantity.
Lens magnification (write it on its own): m = h'/h = v/u; a negative m gives an inverted image and a positive m gives an erect image.

Power of a lens (write it on its own): P = 1/f with f in metres, unit dioptre (D), so 1 D = 1 m^-1; convex lenses have positive power and concave lenses negative power. Examples: f = 50 cm gives P = +2 D; a concave lens of f = 2 m gives P = -0.5 D.

Lenses in contact: powers add algebraically, P = P1 + P2; for +2 D and -0.5 D in contact the net power is +1.5 D and the net focal length is 1/1.5 m = 0.67 m approx, so the combination still converges.

Worked drill: convex lens f = +20 cm with object at u = -30 cm gives 1/v = 1/20 - 1/30 = 1/60, so v = +60 cm and m = v/u = 60/(-30) = -2: a real, inverted image twice as tall, 60 cm on the other side.
Common mistake: mixing centimetres and metres in P = 1/f; convert focal length to metres BEFORE taking the reciprocal, and check the sign of the answer against the expected nature of the image.

keyTerms.meaning: The degree of convergence or divergence produced by a lens, P = 1/f in metres, unit dioptre.
SI unit of lens power; a lens of focal length 1 m has a power of 1 D.
1/v - 1/u = 1/f for a thin lens, used with the Cartesian sign convention.

sections.trick: PADD: Powers ADD when lenses touch. P = 1/f works only with f in METRES: 1 D = 1 m^-1. Positive P converges, negative P diverges.
sections.examPointer: The 5-mark numerical usually chains image distance, magnification, image height and lens power; present it as given-formula-substitution-answer and end by stating the nature of the image to collect full step marks.

mcqs.question: A ray of light falls normally on a plane mirror. The angle of reflection is:
mcqs.explanation: On normal incidence the ray retraces its path: the angle of incidence is 0, and since angle i = angle r the angle of reflection is also 0.

mcqs.question: Which mirror is used as a rear-view mirror in vehicles?
mcqs.explanation: A convex mirror always gives an erect, diminished image with a wide field of view, so the driver can see a large area of traffic behind in a small mirror.

mcqs.question: The SI unit of the power of a lens is:
mcqs.explanation: P = 1/f with f in metres gives the unit dioptre; 1 D = 1 m^-1.

mcqs.question: The focal length of a plane mirror is:
mcqs.explanation: A plane mirror may be treated as a spherical mirror of infinite radius of curvature, so from f = R/2 its focal length is infinity.

mcqs.question: An object is placed 10 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. The image formed is:
mcqs.explanation: u = -10 cm, f = -15 cm: 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = -1/15 + 1/10 = 1/30, so v = +30 cm behind the mirror and m = -v/u = +3, a virtual, erect, 3 times enlarged image.

mcqs.question: The refractive index of water is 4/3. The speed of light in water is:
An object is placed 30 cm from a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. The image distance is:
mcqs.explanation: 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/20 - 1/30 = 1/60, so v = +60 cm; m = v/u = 60/(-30) = -2, so the image is real, inverted and enlarged.

mcqs.question: A lens has a power of -2.0 D. The lens and its focal length are:
mcqs.explanation: f = 1/P = 1/(-2) m = -0.5 m = -50 cm; the negative power shows a diverging, that is a concave, lens.

mcqs.question: A 3 cm tall object is placed 18 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 12 cm. The image is:
options: 36 cm in front of the mirror, 6 cm tall, real and inverted
36 cm behind the mirror, 6 cm tall, virtual and erect
24 cm in front of the mirror, 4 cm tall, real and inverted
9 cm behind the mirror, 1.5 cm tall, virtual and erect
mcqs.explanation: 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = -1/12 + 1/18 = -1/36, so v = -36 cm; m = -v/u = -(-36)/(-18) = -2, so h' = -2 × 3 = -6 cm: real, inverted and doubled in size.

mcqs.question: Two thin lenses of power +2.0 D and -0.5 D are kept in contact. The combination behaves as:
options: A converging lens of power +2.5 D
A diverging lens of power -1.5 D
A converging lens of power +1.0 D
A converging lens of power +1.5 D
mcqs.explanation: Powers in contact add: P = +2.0 - 0.5 = +1.5 D; f = 1/P = 1/1.5 m = 0.67 m approx, so the combination still converges.

boardQuestions.question: State the two laws of reflection of light.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. 2) The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (angle i = angle r). Both laws hold for plane and spherical mirrors, and the angles are always measured from the normal, not from the mirror surface.

boardQuestions.question: Describe, with ray diagrams in words, the image formed by a convex mirror when the object is (a) far away from the mirror and (b) close to the mirror, and explain why a convex mirror is preferred as a rear-view mirror in vehicles.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Object far away (nearly at infinity): draw a ray parallel to the principal axis which after reflection appears to come from the focus F behind the mirror, and a ray aimed towards the centre of curvature C which retraces its path; the reflected rays diverge, so the image forms at F behind the mirror, virtual, erect and point-sized (highly diminished). 2) Object close to the mirror: the same two rays meet only when produced backwards, giving an image between P and F behind the mirror, virtual, erect and diminished; for every object position the convex mirror image remains virtual, erect and diminished. 3) Rear-view reasons: because the image is always erect and diminished, a large number of vehicles fit into a small mirror, and the convex shape gives a much wider field of view than a plane mirror of the same size, so the driver can safely watch the traffic behind.

boardQuestions.question: The speed of light in glass is 2 × 10^8 m/s while in vacuum it is 3 × 10^8 m/s. Calculate the refractive index of glass.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: given c = 3 × 10^8 m/s and v = 2 × 10^8 m/s. Step 2: formula n = c/v. Step 3: substitute n = (3 × 10^8)/(2 × 10^8) = 1.5. Answer: refractive index of glass = 1.5, which means light travels 1.5 times slower in glass than in vacuum.

boardQuestions.question: A concave mirror produces a real, inverted image magnified 3 times when an object is placed 10 cm in front of it. Find the position of the image and the focal length of the mirror.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: given u = -10 cm and m = -3, since a real, inverted image has negative magnification. Step 2: formula m = -v/u gives -3 = -v/(-10) = v/10, so v = -30 cm: the image is 30 cm in front of the mirror. Step 3: mirror formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u = 1/(-30) + 1/(-10) = -4/30, so f = -7.5 cm. Answer: image at 30 cm in front of the mirror and focal length 7.5 cm, the negative sign confirming a concave mirror.

boardQuestions.question: An object 5 cm high is placed 25 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Find the position, size and nature of the image.
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: given u = -25 cm, f = +10 cm, h = +5 cm. Step 2: lens formula 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/10 - 1/25 = 3/50, so v = 50/3 = 16.7 cm approx; the positive v means the image is real and forms 16.7 cm on the other side of the lens. Step 3: magnification m = v/u = (50/3)/(-25) = -2/3 = -0.67 approx, so h' = m × h = -3.3 cm approx. Answer: a real, inverted, diminished image about 16.7 cm behind the lens and about 3.3 cm tall.

boardQuestions.question: Describe with labelled ray diagrams (explain each ray you draw in words) the image formed by a concave mirror when the object is (a) beyond C, (b) at C and (c) between F and C, and state the nature of the image in each case.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Object beyond C: draw a ray parallel to the principal axis which after reflection passes through F, and a second ray through C which retraces its path; the two reflected rays meet between F and C, so the image is between F and C, real, inverted and diminished. 2) Object at C: use the same two rays; they meet at C itself, so the image is at C, real, inverted and of the same size (m = -1). 3) Object between F and C: the reflected rays meet beyond C, so the image is beyond C, real, inverted and enlarged. 4) Remember the fourth case as well: object between P and F gives a virtual, erect, enlarged image behind the mirror, the shaving-mirror arrangement.

boardQuestions.question: CASE: In the laboratory a student finds the focal length of a concave mirror by the sharp-image method using a distant object and gets 20 cm. She then places a burning candle 5 cm tall on the principal axis, 30 cm from the pole of the mirror. Answer: (a) Where should the screen be placed to get a sharp image? (b) Find the magnification and the height of the image and state its nature. (c) If the candle is moved to 15 cm from the mirror, what happens to the image and can it still be caught on a screen?
boardQuestions.answer: Step 1: given f = -20 cm, u = -30 cm, h = +5 cm. Step 2: mirror formula 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = -1/20 + 1/30 = -1/60, so v = -60 cm; for (a) the screen must be placed 60 cm in front of the mirror. Step 3: magnification m = -v/u = -(-60)/(-30) = -2, so h' = m × h = -10 cm; for (b) the image is 10 cm tall, inverted and enlarged, and being real it can be caught on the screen. Step 4: for (c), at u = -15 cm the object lies between F and P, and 1/v = -1/20 + 1/15 = 1/60 gives v = +60 cm with m = -v/u = +4; the image is virtual, erect and 4 times enlarged, 60 cm behind the mirror, and NO screen can catch it because the reflected rays only appear to meet there. Answer: (a) screen 60 cm in front of the mirror, (b) m = -2, image 10 cm tall, real and inverted, (c) a virtual, erect, enlarged image 60 cm behind the mirror, not catchable on a screen.

chapters.title: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
chapters.summary: The human eye forms a real, inverted image on the retina and changes its focal length through the ciliary muscles for accommodation between the near point of 25 cm and a far point of infinity. Defects of vision and their lens corrections are followed by dispersion of white light by a prism, atmospheric refraction effects and scattering of light phenomena.

Power of accommodation, near point and far point

Dispersion by a prism and the VIBGYOR spectrum
